title: Ki Hajar Dewantara: the teacher who opened doors
text:
Every year on 2 May, schools across Indonesia celebrate National Education Day. The date was chosen because it is the birthday of Ki Hajar Dewantara, a writer and teacher who believed that every child deserved a good education.

He was born in Yogyakarta in 1889 and was first named Raden Mas Soewardi Soerjaningrat. His family belonged to the Javanese nobility, so he was able to go to school. At that time, Indonesia was ruled by the Netherlands, and very few Indonesian children had the chance to learn to read and write.

As a young man, Soewardi began training to be a doctor, but illness forced him to leave his course. He became a journalist instead. His articles were sharp and brave. In 1913, he wrote an article called “If I Were a Dutchman”. In it, he criticised the colonial government for asking Indonesians to help pay for a celebration of Dutch independence, while Indonesia itself was not free. The government was furious, and as a punishment, he was sent away to the Netherlands.

He turned his exile into an opportunity. While he was in the Netherlands, he studied education and earned a teaching certificate. He also read about new ideas in teaching that put children’s interests and talents at the centre of learning.

He returned home in 1919, ready to put these ideas into practice. In 1922, he opened a school in Yogyakarta called Taman Siswa, which means “Garden of Pupils”. Its lessons included Indonesian music, dance and culture as well as modern subjects, and it was open to children from ordinary families. Soon there were Taman Siswa schools in many towns.

Later, he changed his name to Ki Hajar Dewantara and stopped using his noble title, so that he could be closer to ordinary people. When Indonesia became independent in 1945, he was appointed the country’s first Minister of Education.

Ki Hajar Dewantara died in 1959. His most famous saying describes how a good teacher should behave: in front, set an example; in the middle, build their spirit; behind, give encouragement. The last part, “Tut Wuri Handayani”, still appears on the logo of Indonesia’s education ministry.
